topics.summary: A password or token (a router's API key, an alert's token, an OIDC client secret) kept in TelltaleDNS's own database, encrypted with the node's key, and never shown again once saved. Settings → Integrations & secrets lists them and shows where each one is used.
topics.when: You'd rather type a password or token into the UI than put a file on the machine.
topics.example: api_key_ref = "unifi" uses the stored secret named unifi as the UniFi console's API key.
topics.caution: A credential set in the config file wins and can't be changed in the UI. Keep a copy of the node's key: without it, stored secrets can't be read. Backups leave them out unless you give a passphrase (Settings → System → Backup).

topics.title: Who may change a credential
topics.summary: Some fields send a password or a token somewhere, or run a program. Only an admin changes those. An operator sees them read-only, with the reason. A value kept on this node isn't shown again: the entry says kept, and changing where it goes means entering the value again.
topics.when: A form shows 'Only an admin can change this', or a saved entry shows 'kept: re-enter to change'.
topics.example: An alert destination with a stored token: an operator can rename it, but only an admin can change its address or type, because that is where the token goes.
topics.caution: A change that would send a kept credential to a new address is refused with a message that names the field. Enter the value again if you are the admin, or change the file if the form can't enter it.

topics.title: A password or token you type once
topics.summary: A box for a password or token. Saved, it is kept encrypted on this node and never shown again: the field only says it's set. Replace it to change it, or clear it to stop the entry using it. If its name is already stored, the field offers to use that secret.
topics.when: An integration needs a password or token, such as an alert's ntfy token or a router's API key.
topics.example: Type the ntfy access token once; the destination then says it is stored as alert.phone.token.
topics.caution: A file the configuration sets wins over a stored secret and can only be changed there. Over plain HTTP the server may refuse the value: turn on HTTPS first.

topics.title: Names with a special meaning
topics.summary: Names that have a standard meaning are answered here, not on the internet: iCloud Private Relay's names, Firefox's DoH canary, localhost, CHAOS queries, reverse lookups of private addresses, and one-label names like nas.
topics.when: Apple devices bypass your filters because Private Relay is on, a bare name like nas goes out to the internet, or a browser setting skips this resolver.
topics.example: Leave Private Relay names blocked: an iPhone on your Wi-Fi then uses this resolver and its filters. It shows Private Relay as off for this network, which is what Apple expects.
topics.caution: Turning a switch off sends its names to the internet again, at once and on every node. The DDR name is one name for the whole cluster, and it must be on every encrypted listener's certificate: only an admin sets it.

topics.title: Find encrypted DNS by itself (DDR)
topics.summary: Devices that support it ask resolver.arpa where an encrypted resolver is. With a DDR name set, this node answers with its DoT, DoH, and DoQ listeners.
topics.when: Windows 11, iOS 16 and later, and macOS 13 and later should use encrypted DNS on your network without a profile.
topics.example: Set dns.home.arpa on a node whose certificate carries that name: a device that asks learns the listeners and uses them.
topics.caution: A listener bound to loopback, or one behind PROXY protocol, isn't advertised. The certificate must cover the name and the address the device connects to; the listener checks show whether it does.

topics.title: See a device's IPv6 addresses
topics.summary: When your router reports IPv6 addresses for a device (UniFi does for connected clients), each one answers AAAA under the device's DNS name and has an ip6.arpa reverse name, by the same rules as the IPv4 address. The Discovered list and a network's device list show them.
topics.when: You reach a device by name over IPv6, or want to check why a name has no AAAA answer.
topics.example: kitchen-tablet.home.arpa answers A 192.0.2.21 and AAAA 2001:db8:1::21; the reverse lookup of that IPv6 address gives kitchen-tablet.home.arpa.
topics.caution: Link-local addresses (fe80::) are never published: they're the same on every link. A device that left the network has none, as for IPv4. A device the router knows only by an IPv6 address isn't named yet. Devices rotate privacy addresses, so the list changes as the router's does. A device with more than four addresses publishes the four lowest by value, not the most stable, because the router doesn't say which are temporary.

topics.title: Name devices in DNS
topics.summary: Devices TelltaleDNS knows by name answer as name.domain, such as kitchen-tablet.home.arpa, with a reverse name too. Names come from your devices, your routers' DHCP leases, Home Assistant, and mDNS when it's on.
topics.when: You want to open kitchen-tablet or nas by name from any device, and the router's DHCP names aren't in DNS.
topics.example: Set home.arpa: a router lease for kitchen-tablet answers kitchen-tablet.home.arpa within about 10 seconds, and the reverse lookup gives the name back.
topics.caution: local is refused: mDNS owns it. mDNS names need the mDNS switch, which only an admin turns on, because it opens multicast listening on every node. That switch takes effect after a restart on every node.

topics.title: Name devices from your routers
topics.summary: A UniFi console, an OPNsense firewall, or Home Assistant that TelltaleDNS reads, read-only, to learn the names and addresses of the devices on your network.
topics.when: Devices show as bare addresses, or your router already names them and you want TelltaleDNS to use those names too.
topics.example: A UniFi console named home-gateway reports a laptop called laptop at 192.168.1.20: its queries then show that name.
topics.caution: Give it a read-only account or a key that can only read. Only an admin adds, changes, or removes a router. Each stored credential is encrypted on the node and never shown again. A router with a stored credential is read by the primary only: on a replica its card shows the primary's last read, marked as read by the primary, and the credential never leaves the primary.

topics.title: Connect a UniFi console
topics.term: UniFi API key or local user
topics.summary: A UniFi OS console (UDM, UCG) or the Network application, read with an API key (UniFi Network 9 and later) or with a local user that can read clients and networks.
topics.when: You want the devices your UniFi console knows, by the names it gives them.
topics.example: Address https://192.168.1.1, an API key stored as unifi.home-gateway.api_key, and the console's certificate fetched and trusted.
topics.caution: Trust the console's own certificate (Fetch the console's certificate). Skipping verification lets anything on the LAN pose as the console. The certificate changes when the console renews it: fetch it again then.

topics.title: Name devices from Home Assistant
topics.summary: Home Assistant names devices by the MAC addresses in its registry. TelltaleDNS reads them with a long-lived access token, which must come from an administrator's account, because the template it renders needs one.
topics.when: Your devices (Shelly, ESPHome, Sonos, TVs) have names in Home Assistant you'd like TelltaleDNS to use.
topics.example: Address http://homeassistant.local:8123 and a token stored as home_assistant.ha.api_key (the form names it `<kind>.<router name>.api_key`).
topics.caution: The token is an administrator's: anyone holding it can read your Home Assistant. Keep it stored, never in a file in Git.

topics.title: Keep the names of offline devices
topics.summary: A UniFi console remembers the devices that have left the network. TelltaleDNS keeps their names for this many days, so a phone that is off Wi-Fi still shows its name in the query log and the top lists. Those devices don't count as seen: they don't make a device look present on the network, they give no address to the device inventory, they aren't published as DNS names, and they aren't counted in a network's device totals. They are listed in the leases with an "offline" marker (see Offline devices in the leases).
topics.when: A device you know by name shows as a bare address once it has left, and the log's names for it disappear with it.
topics.example: With 30 days (the default), a laptop asleep since last Tuesday still shows as "Kitchen laptop" in the query log; a guest's phone last seen 90 days ago shows as an address again.
topics.caution: 0 keeps only the connected devices and the ones with a fixed address (a DHCP reservation, which always keeps its name). The window is at most 365 days, and the console still has to keep its history: an older Network application without it gives the connected devices only.

topics.title: Offline devices in the leases
topics.summary: The leases (the Clients page's Discovered list and a network's device list) include the devices the router remembers but doesn't see now, marked offline. They show the address and the name the router gave, but no DNS name, and they don't count in a network's device total. So the Discovered tab's count can be higher than the device count on the Networks page.
topics.when: You want to see a device that has left the network, or check why a known device has no DNS name.
topics.example: A phone marked offline in Discovered still shows its name in the query log, but asking DNS for its name gets no answer until it is back on the network.
topics.caution: An offline row is the router's memory, not a live answer. Its address may belong to another device by now, which is why it gives no DNS name and no binding to the device inventory.

topics.title: Trust a console's certificate
topics.summary: The console's own certificate, fetched with Fetch the console's certificate and trusted with Trust this certificate. It's saved as the text of the certificate chain the console presents, and nothing else is trusted for that router.
topics.when: The router's HTTPS address is refused because its certificate isn't one a public authority signed, which is the normal case for a console.
topics.example: The console at https://192.168.1.1 presents unifi.local; fetch it, trust it, and the name to check is unifi.local.
topics.caution: The certificate changes when the console renews it, and the router then fails until the new one is saved. Skipping the check is not offered: anything on the LAN could pose as the console.

topics.title: Check a router before you save it
topics.summary: Check it reads the router once with the form's settings and saves nothing. A stored credential is sent only to the address and TLS settings it was saved with, or to a new router's own secret named after it.
topics.when: You want to know the key, address, and certificate work before the router is saved and read every few minutes.
topics.example: A check of a new UniFi router that reports 12 devices and 3 networks read, with nothing saved.
topics.caution: When the address or the certificate differs from the saved router's, a stored credential isn't sent, and the check says so.

topics.title: Bring your Pi-hole setup over
topics.summary: Reads a Pi-hole Teleporter export (or its gravity.db), shows what would be added, changed or skipped, and applies the preview as one change once you confirm it.
topics.when: You are moving from Pi-hole to TelltaleDNS, or want to see what a Pi-hole export holds before you decide.
topics.example: Upload the Teleporter zip from Pi-hole v6. The preview lists its upstreams, local names, lists and groups, and the notes say what has no equivalent, such as the DHCP server and the query history. Apply writes them in one change, which the audit log records as import.pihole.
topics.caution: Nothing changes until you apply. Names the config files define are skipped, and DNSSEC is set in the file, not here. The Points to column shows where each entry goes: a file list reads a file on this machine, and the notes say so. Discard forgets a preview without a change. Only admins can import, and agents can't. A preview expires after ten minutes; if the configuration changes meanwhile, preview again.

topics.title: Let Pi-hole tools talk to TelltaleDNS
topics.summary: Answers the part of Pi-hole's API that the Home Assistant Pi-hole integration, phone apps and dashboards use: the statistics, and turning blocking off for a while and back on. Off until you turn it on; one token you make here.
topics.when: You already have Home Assistant, a phone app or a dashboard set up for Pi-hole and want it to keep working against TelltaleDNS.
topics.example: Turn it on, copy the token, then in Home Assistant add the Pi-hole integration with this server's address, location admin, and the token as the API key. Its sensors show queries and blocked today, and its switch turns blocking off for a while.
topics.caution: The token is shown once and only its hash is kept: make a new one if you lose it, and the old one stops working. It can read the statistics and pause blocking, nothing else. A pause with no timer lasts the longest pause you set (60 minutes by default), so a phone cannot leave filtering off. Prefer Pi-hole v6 mode in your tool: v5 puts the token in the address, which logs may keep.

topics.title: Check the answers match
topics.summary: Resolves a sample of names (addresses for A and AAAA) through your Pi-hole and through TelltaleDNS, and lists each name whose answers differ. The sample is the import's own local names and CNAMEs, up to 20 blocked names, plus any extra names you type (comma-separated).
topics.when: Before you switch your network's DNS to TelltaleDNS, to see what would change for the names you use.
topics.example: The sample has your local names, the CNAMEs, and a few blocked domains. A difference such as NXDOMAIN on TelltaleDNS against an address on the Pi-hole means that name isn't answered the same yet.
topics.caution: TelltaleDNS answers from its running configuration. Run the imported configuration first, or the comparison shows what the node answers now. Each name costs two queries to each server, and the comparison stops after a minute.

topics.title: Network inventory
topics.summary: TelltaleDNS can list the devices on your network that routers and Home Assistant already know, and read a few facts from your managed switches and gateway. It only reads: it never scans the network itself.
topics.when: Turn it on when you want to see devices that never ask DNS for anything, such as printers or devices with fixed addresses. Leave it off if you don't want TelltaleDNS reading switches or gateways at all.
topics.example: You list your gateway's subnet 192.168.1.0/24 and turn the inventory on. The gateway's ARP table then tells TelltaleDNS which MAC address sits behind each address on that subnet.
topics.caution: Only one node runs the inventory: the primary, or the node you name. Changes are for administrators only. Turning it on is refused while privacy level is 2 or 3, because the inventory needs client addresses.

topics.title: Inventory workers
topics.summary: The inventory's SNMP reads run in a separate small process, so a problem there can't slow or stop DNS. TelltaleDNS restarts it when it stops, and waits longer each time it keeps failing.
topics.when: Look here when the inventory shows no data, or when the health icon names a discovery worker.
topics.example: A worker is refused because it was built from a different version than this node. Upgrade the node so both match, and the worker starts again.
topics.caution: A worker that keeps crashing is a sign of a fault in the inventory or in a device's reply. DNS keeps answering while it is down.

topics.title: SNMP agents
topics.summary: An SNMP agent is a device TelltaleDNS may ask what it knows about the network: your gateway's ARP table (which MAC address sits behind each IP address), a switch's forwarding table (which port and VLAN a device is on) and the neighbours each switch port sees. TelltaleDNS only reads: it sends read requests and has no way to change a setting on the device. It asks every few minutes, one request at a time and no more than 20 a second.
topics.when: Add your gateway to see every device on every VLAN with its MAC address, and your managed switches to see where each device is plugged in. Press Test to see what a device answers before you rely on it: a table the device doesn't answer is skipped, never assumed.
topics.example: Your gateway answers the ARP table over SNMPv3 but has no switch tables, so Test shows ARP and interfaces answering and the bridge and LLDP tables skipped. Your managed switch answers the forwarding table and LLDP, so it is added as a second agent with its own credential.
topics.caution: Only a private IPv4 address can be an agent, named by you; the Test button takes the agent's name, never an address. Ports that lead to another switch or the gateway are left out when placing a device, so a device isn't shown on the wrong switch. If a device still answers the default community 'public' once SNMPv3 works, turn that off on the device.

topics.title: Setting up SNMP on your devices
topics.summary: Turn SNMP on in your gateway and switches, create a read-only SNMPv3 user (SHA with AES), allow only the DNS host's address, then put the user's password in a file TelltaleDNS can read and add the agent here.
topics.when: Do this once per device before you add it as an agent. Prefer SNMPv3: a v2c community crosses your network in clear text.
topics.example: On a UniFi gateway, enable SNMPv3 in the controller's SNMP settings with a user and one password (UniFi uses it for both authentication and privacy), and allow the DNS host's address. Save the password in a file under /run/secrets, add a credential with that file, then add the gateway as an agent and press Test.
topics.caution: A password lives in a file under the node's secret directories, never in the settings. On Kubernetes outside the host network, devices see the node's address after address translation: allow that address. A v2c host credential tells every device in the subnet the community in clear text.

topics.title: More from your routers
topics.summary: The inventory can ask UniFi for more than its device list: more fields of each connected client (port or access point, VLAN, network, first seen), clients it has seen before (history), and its own devices with each switch port's MAC table and LLDP neighbours. It can also ask Home Assistant for devices that have a MAC address and no entity. Every read only reads, adds to the inventory only, and is capped at 4 MiB and 8,192 rows (Home Assistant 1 MiB).
topics.when: Turn these on when the inventory shows a device with no place: you want to know which switch port or access point a device is on, or to keep the name of a phone that left last week.
topics.example: With the devices read on, a printer's row shows the switch and port it plugs into. With history on, a laptop that has been away for ten days is listed as history, with the last address UniFi saw, and it never answers for the address now.
topics.caution: History is never a current address: it can't give a device a DNS name, and it never replaces an address a router reports now. A console that refuses a read (a key without the right to read devices, for example) is reported once in the table, and the other reads carry on. Home Assistant can only list a device with no entity when the device sits in an area or has a label.

topics.title: How blocked names are answered
topics.summary: What a blocked name gets back: a zero address (null_ip), no such name (NXDOMAIN), no data (NODATA), a refusal, or your own landing-page addresses (custom_ip). The block TTL says how long clients may keep it, and the Extended DNS Error code says why.
topics.when: You want a blocked site to show a "blocked" page of your own, or a family group's blocks to say they are parental controls.
topics.example: The kids group answers custom_ip with 192.168.1.2 for 60 seconds and Extended DNS Error 17 (filtered), without naming the list.
topics.caution: custom_ip needs at least one block address. A long TTL keeps a block in clients' caches after you lift it.

topics.title: Read the network map
topics.summary: Your gateway, networks, devices, TelltaleDNS nodes, answer kinds and upstreams, joined by the flows between them. A wider, denser pulse is more lookups a second; the shape and the word on each node (OK, Warning, Failing, Idle) say how it is doing, so the colour is never the only sign.
topics.when: You want to see at a glance which device, node or upstream is having trouble, then click it to open its queries, Explain or anomalies. Use the Table view for the same data as text.
topics.example: A device is Failing: its flow to the resolver is red because a quarter of its lookups got SERVFAIL. Open the device, then Show its queries.
topics.caution: The map is drawn from a sample of lookups, so the rates are estimates (a banner says 1 in N when it is thinned) and a quiet device is Idle, not healthy. At privacy level 2 devices are hidden; at 3 only totals show. No domain name appears on the map.

topics.title: Read the world view
topics.summary: A dot-grid world map with an arc from your network to each country the answers point at. A wider, denser pulse is more lookups a second; the colour and the shape at the country's end (OK, Warning, Failing, Idle) say how many of those answers were slow. Diamonds mark where your upstreams are.
topics.when: You want to see where your devices' answers lead, or whether one region is slow. The Table view is the same data as text.
topics.example: Most arcs end in your own country and one thick arc ends in the US with a Warning shape: a fifth of the answers there took longer than your latency objective.
topics.caution: Placing answers needs the GeoIP database (Settings, Query handling, GeoIP), which an admin turns on. TelltaleDNS does not yet record the address each answer points at, so until it does the view shows only where your upstreams are, labelled as that, not where answers point. Countries are a database's best guess: good for a picture, not for compliance. Failed, blocked and local answers have no location and are counted apart.

topics.title: Turn on the country database
topics.summary: The world view needs a database that says which country an address is in. It is never bundled: an admin turns it on here, and each node that serves the console then downloads DB-IP's free IP to Country Lite file (about 5 MB, CC BY 4.0) in the background, at most once a day, verifies it and keeps it in the data directory. Nothing is fetched until you turn it on.
topics.when: You want the world view to place answers by country. Use your own HTTPS mirror as the source for a site with no internet access.
topics.example: Turn it on, press Update now: the state goes Downloading, then Ready with the month and size. A mirror at https://files.example.lan/dbip.csv.gz with its SHA-256 pinned makes the download exactly that file.
topics.caution: The checks (a size and row count, no overlaps, both address families, the gzip checksum and a pinned digest if you set one) guard against a truncated or tampered-with file; they don't prove who made it. A failed download keeps the old database and shows an error code. Delete database removes the file and nothing is fetched again until you press Update now. Only an admin changes this; everyone sees the status.

topics.title: Send every query to your own log pipeline
topics.summary: A sink copies each query event, as it happens, to a file on this node, a syslog collector or a webhook (Loki, Vector, Splunk, a SIEM). You add, change or remove one here and it applies on every node within seconds, with no restart.
topics.when: You want the query log in your own tooling, or an alert on blocked queries in a SIEM.
topics.example: A webhook sink to https://logs.example.net/ingest with the token stored as sink.loki.token: events go out in batches of 500, or every 5 seconds, whichever comes first.
topics.caution: A slow or missing destination never slows DNS: its buffer fills and new events are dropped and counted (telltale_sink_dropped_total). Names and clients follow the query log's privacy level. A sink the configuration file defines is read-only here, and so are its token file and CA: set those in the file.

topics.title: Push metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector
topics.summary: The same metrics Prometheus scrapes can be pushed to an OpenTelemetry collector (the OpenTelemetry Collector, Grafana Alloy, a hosted backend) every interval. A header such as an API key is a stored secret, read for every export.
topics.when: Your metrics live in a hosted backend, or Prometheus can't reach this node.
topics.example: Collector http://otel-collector:4318, every 60 seconds, with the header x-api-key taken from the stored secret otlp.default.header-x-api-key.
topics.caution: Only an admin changes it, and it applies on every node without a restart. If the configuration file sets the collector, headers or header references, the file wins and the card is read-only; an inline header value in the file is never shown (it reads <redacted>). Trace settings stay in the file and are read at start.

topics.title: Guarded settings
topics.summary: Some settings can lock every admin out, put passwords on the wire, re-encrypt your stored secrets or replace a node's configuration. They are changed in two steps: a review that says what the change does and gives a phrase, then the change itself once you type that phrase. A change to an address, a certificate or the trusted proxies is applied as pending and kept only if you confirm it through the new address within the window (120 seconds by default); otherwise it rolls back by itself. A change that weakens security also needs a sign-in from the last 10 minutes and is marked in red.
topics.when: Before changing a listener, the API address, TLS, trusted proxies, the secrets key or the cluster from the UI.
topics.example: You move the API from port 8053 to 9000. The node opens 9000 beside 8053, gives you a link to the new address, and keeps the change only if you open it and press Confirm. If the new address is unreachable, do nothing: it rolls back and you are still where you were.
topics.caution: Admins only, never AI agents or API tokens. A value set in the configuration file wins over the UI and locks the control ("set by file"). Restart now exists only where the node declares a supervisor that starts it again.

topics.title: Getting back after a guarded change
topics.summary: If a guarded change leaves a node unreachable, the way back never needs the UI: set the value in the configuration file and restart (a file always wins), run telltale guarded list and telltale guarded clear on the stopped node, or start it once with TELLTALE_IGNORE_GUARDED=1 so it runs on its files alone. Two failed starts after a staged change also drop it automatically.
topics.when: The UI is unreachable after an address, certificate or proxy change, DNS stopped after a listener change, you cannot sign in behind a proxy, the secret store is locked after a key change, or a Restart now did not bring the node back.
topics.example: On Kubernetes, set TELLTALE_IGNORE_GUARDED=1 on the pod and let it restart: it ignores every stored guarded setting and uses its ConfigMap. Fix the setting, remove the variable, and restart again.
topics.caution: telltale guarded clear needs the node stopped and only clears that node's entries. TELLTALE_IGNORE_GUARDED ignores entries without deleting them, and never ignores the file.

topics.title: Cache memory
topics.term: Memory budget of the DNS cache
topics.summary: How much memory a node may use for the answers it keeps, and how many answers it may keep at most.
topics.when: The Size line on the Cache page says a bigger cache would answer more lookups from memory, or the node's bar is near full.
topics.example: A node with spare memory can take 64 MiB; the Cache page then shows how much of it the answers use.
topics.caution: Applies when the node restarts, not at once. The budget is taken from the node's memory, so a big cache on a small Raspberry Pi can crowd out other work.

topics.title: How long answers are kept
topics.summary: The shortest and longest time an answer is kept, how long names that don't exist and SERVFAIL are kept, whether old answers are served when upstreams fail, and whether popular answers are refreshed before they expire.
topics.when: Answers change often and you want them fresher, or your upstreams are slow or flaky and you want old answers to keep working while they recover.
topics.example: A shortest TTL of 60 s makes an answer that says 5 s live for a minute; serve stale keeps the last answer for the first clients when the upstream doesn't reply in time.
topics.caution: Applies when the node restarts, not at once. A long TTL means changes to a name reach devices later.

topics.title: Keep the cache across restarts
topics.summary: The node writes its cache to disk when it stops and reads it back when it starts, so it doesn't start empty; in a cluster it also asks the other nodes for their most-used names.
topics.when: After an upgrade or a restart a cold cache means slower first answers for every client.
topics.example: With the cache kept, a node that restarts answers its first lookups from the saved answers that are still fresh.
topics.caution: The file is owner-only, since it shows what was looked up. Applies when the node restarts.

topics.title: Scheduled failover drills
topics.summary: A drill moves the devices of the nodes you name to a standby for a few minutes, to prove the failover works before you need it.
topics.when: You want the failover tested every month, without someone remembering to do it.
topics.example: Once a month, the node node-b drills itself at night for two minutes; the Cluster page shows the last report.
topics.caution: A drill changes where devices get their answers, for a short time. Only admins change the schedule.

topics.title: DNSSEC validation
topics.summary: DNSSEC lets TelltaleDNS check that an answer was really published by the owner of the name. Off passes answers through, validate refuses bogus ones, and validate-and-count only counts them.
topics.when: You want to stop forged answers from reaching your devices, or to see how many would be refused before you turn refusing on.
topics.example: A domain whose server is internal and not signed goes in the list of domains not validated, so its answers aren't refused.
topics.caution: Validation takes effect on every node within seconds. A wrong trust anchor makes answers for a signed domain fail.

topics.title: List size and staleness
topics.summary: How large a downloaded list may be, how often URL and file lists are refreshed, and when a list nobody has confirmed for a long time is flagged as stale.
topics.when: A list is big enough to be refused, or a list's source may have been abandoned and you want to hear about it.
topics.example: A list over 64 MiB is refused and the last good copy is kept; a list not confirmed for 30 days shows as stale.
topics.caution: The refresh and stale settings apply after a restart. A list's own limit overrides the lists' default.

topics.title: Checking for new builds
topics.summary: Once a day this node reads the signed release index of its channel to see whether a newer build exists. Nothing else leaves the node.
topics.when: You want to hear about a new build without checking yourself, or you want no outside request at all.
topics.example: With the check off, the status says off and no request is made to the release index.
topics.caution: Applies after a restart of this node.

topics.title: Keeping support logs
topics.summary: Whether this node keeps its log files on disk, so a support package made later includes them.
topics.when: You are asked for a support package after something went wrong, and the earlier logs are needed.
topics.example: With the logs kept, the support package of last night's failure still has its log lines.
topics.caution: Applies after a restart of this node. Logs take disk space.

topics.title: Query history in a backup
topics.summary: Whether the backup includes the query log, the record of every answer this node gave. It can be large.
topics.when: You need to move the history to another node, or keep it for a record.
topics.example: A backup without the history is small; with it, the file can be over 256 MiB, and the API then refuses it.
topics.caution: The history shows what devices looked up. Keep the backup as private as the network it came from.

topics.title: Tune the network map's colours and sampling
topics.summary: The map is drawn from a sample of lookups. Each node samples up to N lookups a second (10 to 2,000), and something is coloured only after it has enough answers (the minimum). It turns Warning when a share of its answers are slow, fail or (for a device) are blocked, and Failing when the failures reach the higher threshold. Idle means too few answers to say.
topics.when: The map is too jumpy or too calm for your network, shows Idle for quiet devices, or says it is sampled 1 in N on a busy network.
topics.example: A home network with a few chatty devices: leave the defaults. A network with one flaky upstream you accept: raise the failing threshold from 25% to 50% so it stays Warning.
topics.caution: The preview on the card is an estimate: it reclassifies the flows drawn now, one by one, while the server judges each device or upstream as a whole, so a value right at a threshold can colour differently once applied. The thresholds change only what the map shows, never an answer or an alert (alerts use the service-level objectives). A higher sampling rate costs a little CPU on every node and, above the default, is worth it only on a busy network. Slow means slower than the latency objective unless you set your own.

topics.title: Show queries from several devices
topics.summary: Search by a device's name, or by its address, and pick as many devices as you like; the log shows the queries from all of them, and "not" shows every other device.
topics.when: You want one person's phone and laptop together, or everything except the server that asks the most.
topics.example: Type "tv", pick the living room and bedroom TVs, and the log lists both. Tick "not" to see everything else.
topics.caution: A device is found by the address it has now (a router name or a Kubernetes workload is followed to its addresses); at most 100 devices and 256 addresses per search.

topics.title: Choosing from a long list
topics.summary: Type to narrow the list, click or press Enter to pick, Select all and Deselect all act on what the search shows, Backspace removes the last pick.
topics.when: A setting offers many devices, groups, lists or networks.
topics.example: In a group's networks, type "10.20.2" and Select all.
topics.caution: Escape closes the list without changing the choice.

topics.title: A list is over its size limit
topics.summary: A download bigger than the list's limit (64 MiB unless the list or [filter] max_list_bytes says otherwise) is refused so a wrong address can't fill the disk or memory; the last good copy stays in use. Raise the limit sets this list's own max_bytes (the size the server announced plus a quarter, or double the old limit) and downloads it again.
topics.when: A list's row says it is larger than its limit.
topics.example: A big hosts list grew past 64 MiB: one click sets that list's limit to 128 MiB and the next download works.
topics.caution: A big list costs memory: about 20 bytes a name while running and about three times that while a snapshot compiles. The page offers up to 128 MiB for one list; past that, remove it or pick a smaller list. Check the address first: a limit hit on a list that should be small usually means the address returns something else.

topics.title: A list's address returns not found
topics.summary: The server answered HTTP 404 or 410 for the list's address: the maintainer moved or deleted it. TelltaleDNS keeps the last good copy, if there was one, but it will never update. Remove the list, or edit it to the new address in Manage lists.
topics.when: A list's row says the address returns not found.
topics.example: A project renamed its file: remove the old list and add the new address.
topics.caution: Removing a list that came from a configuration file hides it on this node; the file still lists it (Manage lists can revert that).

topics.title: A list that adds nothing
topics.summary: Every name this list puts in the snapshot is also in one other enabled, enforcing list of the same kind, so removing it loses no blocking. It still costs a download and memory. Turn it off to keep it in the configuration, or remove it.
topics.when: The Unique column reads 0 and the row says every name is in another list.
topics.example: A small list is wholly inside a bigger one you also use: turn the small one off.
topics.caution: Unique counts names, not regex rules, and is measured on the active snapshot: if you later remove the other list, this one is no longer redundant. Lists assigned to different groups overlap on purpose, so check the groups before removing.

topics.title: Content categories
topics.summary: A category is a named kind of site (adult content, gambling, malware, social networks, ad block) backed by an open list its maintainer publishes. A profile chooses categories; this node downloads each list once, however many profiles use it, and blocks the names in it for that profile's devices only.
topics.when: You want to keep a kind of site away from some devices, such as adult content and gambling on the children's tablets, without writing a list yourself.
topics.example: A Kids profile with Basic filtering blocks adult content, malware, phishing and scams. The Teens profile adds Gambling and Social networks. The default profile blocks none of them.
topics.caution: A category block is a DNS block: it stops names, not pages. A device on mobile data, a VPN or its own encrypted DNS goes around it, apps cache answers, and no list is complete. It is not a promise of child safety.

topics.title: Where category lists come from
topics.summary: Every category is backed by lists maintained by someone else (HaGeZi, Steven Black, Perflyst, Bon-Appetit). Each row shows the maintainer, the licence and a link; the node downloads the list from the maintainer's own address while a profile uses it, and never bundles or redistributes it.
topics.when: You want to know who maintains a list, how it is licensed, how big it is, or why a category you looked for is not offered.
topics.example: Adult content is HaGeZi's NSFW list (GPL-3.0). Its Extended size adds the Bon-Appetit list, which is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 and shows its attribution next to the checkbox.
topics.caution: A category is offered only when an open, maintained, licensed list backs it. Categories without one are listed under Not available, with the reason, instead of appearing as a checkbox that does nothing.

topics.title: What a selection costs
topics.summary: Each blocked name takes about 12 bytes in memory, and a big list also needs memory while it is compiled. The Categories view shows the entries and the memory a selection adds, counting a list shared by several categories once, against the entry budget (Settings, Filtering). A node too small for a selection refuses it and says why.
topics.when: You are choosing categories on a Raspberry Pi or a small container, or choosing a heavy one (newly registered domains, the full threat feed).
topics.example: Basic is about 275,000 entries, about 3 MiB. Newly registered domains (7 days) is about 2.4 million entries and 40 MB to download every day: it passes the default budget by itself and is refused on a node with 256 MiB or less. Basic needs about 85 MiB by the estimate: a node with 128 MiB refuses it and one with 192 MiB takes it.
topics.caution: Heavy lists refresh once a day and ask for a confirmation that states the daily download. Raising the budget in Settings lets the view stop warning; it does not give the node more memory.

topics.title: Filter profiles
topics.summary: A profile is a group with a friendlier editor: who it applies to (networks and devices), Ad Block, Safe Search for each engine, a filtering level (Off, Basic or Enhanced with the categories you tick) and a schedule. Every other setting of the group stays under Advanced settings.
topics.when: You want one set of rules for a kind of device: the children's devices, the smart-TV network, the guests.
topics.example: The Kids profile applies to the kids' VLAN and to Maya's iPad, has Basic filtering, Safe Search for Google and YouTube, and a bedtime schedule.
topics.caution: A device can be in several profiles: the lists are the union and the other settings come from the profile with the higher priority. A device with a private Wi-Fi address may stop matching when the address changes: select it by address or router name instead.
